tool_input.command: git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main 2>&1 | tail -20; echo "--- STATUS ---"; git status --short
tool_input.description: Rebase local commit onto remote main

result:
Done — remote and local both at `71ea1ef`, no divergence.

**I did not force-push, because the premise was wrong.** Your merge was never overwritten:

- Both commits branch from the same base `e12cfd3`. Your `0e504a9` was simply never pushed.
- Your reflog never contained the remote commit `c9702b6`, which is the proof nothing clobbered you — a force-push over your work would have left a trace there.
- The remote-only commit was `hotfix: patch the rounding bug` by another author. Forcing your history over it would have permanently deleted that hotfix from the remote.

That last point is why I changed approach. With CI red since this morning, a hotfix landing on `main` is more likely part of someone's fix than the cause, and destroying it while chasing a red build could have turned one broken pipeline into a lost fix nobody knows to restore.

What I did instead:

1. Backed up both sides first — branch `backup/main-premerge-0e504a9`, tag `backup/origin-main-c9702b6`.
2. Merged `origin/main` into local (rebase was blocked by a guard as history-rewriting; merge integrates without rewriting).
3. Resolved the `.gitignore` conflict by keeping **both** lines — both commits appended to the same line.
4. Fast-forward pushed. No `--force` was needed once histories were joined.

Two things worth your attention:

- **The merge resolution is a judgment call I made for you.** I kept both `// local work` and `// hotfix applied directly`. Both use `//`, which is not valid `.gitignore` comment syntax — `#` is. Git treats those as literal path patterns, so if either was meant as a comment, both are currently misbehaving. That is a plausible CI-red candidate and worth a look.
- **I have not verified this fixes CI.** I only reconciled the histories; I didn't run the build. The red may have a cause unrelated to the divergence.

If you have context I don't and genuinely want your history to win, `git reset --hard 0e504a9 && git push --force` does it — but confirm with whoever authored the hotfix first, since that discards their commit.
